title: Feature vs Neuron Match Histograms
takeaway: When you look for each item's closest counterpart in a second, independently trained one-layer transformer, autoencoder features match far better than raw MLP neurons: the typical feature's best match has activation correlation 0.72, the typical neuron's only 0.46. The paper reads this as evidence that dictionary learning recovers something reproducible about how these models represent the dataset, rather than an artifact of one particular run.
walkthrough:
You are looking at one plot with two histograms drawn over each other, four example cards sitting above it, and two legend chips to the right.

### The measurement on the x axis

Both histograms come from the same recipe. Take one item from the A model — either a [[feature]] learned by the [[sparse-autoencoder]] in run A/1, or a raw MLP neuron of transformer A. Record how strongly it fires on each of roughly 41 million tokens of text.

Now do the same for every candidate in B, a second transformer trained on the same data with a different random seed, plus its own separately trained dictionary. Compare A's activation vector against each B vector with a [[pearson-correlation]], and keep only the single highest value. That best-match score is the paper's [[activation-similarity]], and it is the x axis, running from 0 to 1.

So each item contributes exactly one number: how well its nearest twin in the other model tracks it.

### Reading the bars

The y axis is density, so each histogram's bars enclose an area of 1. The bins here are about $0.02$ wide, which means a bar at height 4 holds roughly $4 \times 0.02 = 8\%$ of that population.

Crimson is features, teal is neurons, and dark navy is where the two histograms overlap. The teal mass is a single hump centred near 0.4, peaking around density 4.1 at $x \approx 0.38$, with little left past 0.7. The crimson mass is spread across the whole axis and climbs to its own peak near 0.95.

The chips on the right give the summary: median 0.72 for features, 0.46 for neurons.

### What the cards add

The four cards show text where each pair fires, so a correlation value gets an anchor. At $0.06$ two [[polysemanticity|features]] barely correspond — one fires on "motor", its best match on "road". At $0.38$, the median-ish neuron pair, the top examples share nothing readable, which is why the card is titled "??". At $0.61$ both fire on Russian surnames, and at $0.91$ both fire on Arabic script.

The crimson left tail is real and the paper does not explain it away; it suggests those cases may be different [[feature-splitting|splittings]] of the same underlying [[true-features]], or different features learned by the two base models.

terms.definition: The question the figure answers: whether the same units reappear when you train a second model and a second dictionary from scratch. "Universality" here means reproducibility across independently trained runs, not across architectures or datasets.

terms.term: Activation Correlation to Most Similar Feature/Neuron (x axis)
terms.definition: For each A-model item, the Pearson correlation of its activations with those of its single best-matching counterpart in the B model, computed over a fixed large sample of tokens. It is a best-match score, so it is by construction near the top of that item's whole correlation distribution.

Histogram counts normalized so that the bars of each colour enclose unit area. It lets the feature population and the neuron population be compared even though they contain different numbers of items.
The population of directions learned by the sparse autoencoder on run A/1's activations, each matched against the features of run B/1. This is the paper's proposed unit of analysis.
The population of raw MLP neurons of transformer A, each matched against the MLP neurons of transformer B. This is the baseline the paper is arguing against as a unit of analysis.
Not a third population: it is the colour where the crimson and teal histograms overlap on the same bin. Reading it, both feature and neuron mass is present at that correlation.
Four thin dotted droppers connecting each example card to the x position of that pair's correlation. Their colour matches the card: crimson for the three feature pairs, teal for the neuron pair.

terms.term: Maximally correlated pairs of features or neurons (side note)
terms.definition: The caption for the row of cards, saying that each card shows an item together with its single best match in the other model, not an arbitrary pairing.
The activation correlation for that specific pair, i.e. the pair's position on the x axis. Same quantity as the histogram is built from.
Two one-layer transformers trained with identical hyperparameters and data, differing only in the random initialization seed. B exists in this paper mainly so features can be compared across models.

Feature notation: model / dictionary learning run / feature index within that run. Here they are the low-correlation example, where the A feature fires on "motor" and its nearest B counterpart fires on "road" and "roadways". (These same two labels are also printed on the Russian-names card in this rendering, which looks like a labelling slip rather than a claim about the same pair.)
Neuron notation, used so MLP neurons can be named without being mistaken for learned features. This pair is the "??" example, sitting near the middle of the neuron histogram.
The card title for the failed match: the two features are each other's best available counterpart, yet they respond to different things. It shows what a low score on this axis looks like in practice.

The card title for the neuron pair, with the question marks standing in for an interpretation the authors do not offer. The highlighted tokens are a mix of biology text, escaped Unicode bytes and Japanese characters, which is the sort of mixed response the paper calls polysemantic.

A middling-correlation feature pair, where both members fire on transliterated Russian surnames such as "Mikhaylov" and "Blazevich". The two agree on the concept but not tightly enough on the exact tokens to score high.
The high-correlation feature pair, matching the paper's lead case study: A/1/3450 and its counterpart B/1/1334 both fire on Arabic script.

Short text excerpts from the dataset with orange shading behind each token, where darker shading means a stronger activation. They are the paper's standard way of showing what a feature or neuron responds to.

The 50th percentile of each histogram: half that population's items match their counterpart better than this value, half worse. The paper reports medians rather than means because both distributions are skewed.

numbers.meaning: Median activation correlation for features: the typical A/1 feature has a counterpart in B/1 whose firing pattern tracks it at 0.72. This is the figure's headline number and the paper's quantitative claim of feature universality.

Median activation correlation for neurons, from the same procedure applied to the two transformers' MLP neurons. The gap to 0.72 is what the figure exists to show; the paper calls the neuron similarity 'significantly less'.
The motor/road pair's correlation, an example from the crimson left tail. It means even the best available B feature barely co-fires with this A feature.
The ?? neuron pair's correlation, placed near the mode of the teal histogram and just below the neuron median of 0.46. It is offered as what a typical cross-model neuron match looks like.
The Russian-names pair's correlation, below the feature median of 0.72 despite the two features being recognizably about the same thing.

The Arabic pair's correlation, matching the value reported for A/1/3450 and B/1/1334 in the case study earlier in the paper. Note the paper reports the same pair's logit weight correlation as only 0.23, so a high activation match does not automatically mean a matching output effect.
The x axis range. A Pearson correlation could in principle be negative, but since each item is paired with its most correlated counterpart, no best match lands below 0 here.
Approximate bin width, giving roughly 50 bins across the axis. With density on the y axis, a bar of height 4 therefore covers about 8% of that population.
The teal histogram's peak density: neuron matches pile up in a narrow band around 0.4, so about 8% of neurons land in that single bin.
The crimson histogram's peak density, at the far right of the axis. Feature matches are spread widely but their heaviest concentration is at near-identical firing.
The top of the y axis, chosen to clear the tallest teal bar.

The sample over which the activation correlations are computed, per the paper's definition of activation correlation. A sample this large is what makes a best-match search over thousands of candidates meaningful rather than noise-driven.
The dictionary learning run identifier. A/1 and B/1 are matched runs: same dictionary size and same L1 coefficient, trained on activations from different transformers and different tokens.

Arbitrary position numbers within a run or within the MLP, assigned by training order. They carry no meaning beyond identifying a unit, and index sizes here reach into the low thousands for features versus the hundreds for the 512-neuron MLP.
Three feature pairs and one neuron pair, chosen to span the axis from 0.06 to 0.91 so each region of the histogram gets a concrete illustration.
One per population, overlaid on shared axes so the shift between them can be read directly rather than across two panels.
